lessons.title: Modular Monolith and Domain Boundaries
lessons.summary: Modular Monolith First: Domain Boundaries A growing system should first become modular in code and data ownership. A modular monolith keeps one deployment while giving each business capability an explicit public interface. - - - - - HR Payroll Procurement Inventory Accounting Recruitment > >…
lessons.body:
Modular Monolith First: Domain Boundaries
A growing system should first become modular in code and data ownership. A modular monolith keeps one deployment
while giving each business capability an explicit public interface.

-                        -                         -                         -                    -
HR                     Payroll                Procurement                 Inventory                Accounting       Recruitment
>                        >                         >                         >                    >
Figure 2 - Business capabilities become modules, not miscellaneous folders

Module rule
• Group controllers, services, policies, repositories, schemas, and events around a business capability rather than technical type alone.

• Expose only the providers/contracts another module genuinely needs. NestJS modules encapsulate providers by default and exported
providers form the module public interface.

• Avoid making every helper global; controlled imports keep dependency direction visible as the team grows.

When to consider extraction
• Independent scaling profile, independent release cadence, strong data ownership, separate team responsibility, regulatory isolation, or
persistent reliability pressure.

• Do not extract a microservice merely because a module has many files.
apps/api/src/modules/
people/
payroll/
leave/
procurement/
inventory/
accounting/
recruitment/

Each module owns its rules and exports a small public API.

A clean module boundary is valuable even if every module runs in the same NestJS process.
Official reference: NestJS Modules - https://docs.nestjs.com/modules

lessons.summary: Domain Decomposition Blueprints TaskFlow concepts transfer into enterprise domains, but the nouns and invariants change. Model the business capability first, then reuse the architectural patterns. Domain Core records High-value invariants HRIS Employee, Position, Department, Employment active employment, effective dates, manager/department consistency Payroll PayrollRun, PayItem, Deduction,…
lessons.body:
Domain Decomposition Blueprints
TaskFlow concepts transfer into enterprise domains, but the nouns and invariants change. Model the business
capability first, then reuse the architectural patterns.

Domain                           Core records                                       High-value invariants

HRIS                             Employee, Position, Department, Employment         active employment, effective dates, manager/department
consistency

Payroll                          PayrollRun, PayItem, Deduction, Payslip            one finalized result per run/employee, immutable finalized
amounts

Procurement                      Requisition, Quotation, PurchaseOrder, Receipt     approval thresholds, PO state, received quantity <=
ordered quantity

Inventory                        Item, Warehouse, StockMovement, Reservation        ledger consistency, reservation rules, no unauthorized
stock movement

Accounting                       JournalEntry, Account, Period                      balanced debits/credits, closed-period protection

Recruitment                      JobOpening, Applicant, Interview, Offer            stage transitions, role-based access, offer approval

Transferable TaskFlow patterns
• State transitions become approval/workflow policies.

• Workspace membership becomes department/company/branch scope.

• Task audit history becomes payroll, stock, approval, and financial audit evidence.

• Attachment handling becomes contracts, receipts, resumes, payslips, and supporting documents.
Do not create a single "EnterpriseService." Each business capability needs a clear owner.
Source basis: TaskFlow architecture transfer and domain-modeling synthesis; domain policies must be validated against the target organization.

lessons.title: Approval Workflows and Long Running Processes
lessons.summary: Approval Workflows and Long-Running Processes Enterprise systems contain processes that live longer than one HTTP request. Model the workflow explicitly instead of scattering booleans such as approved=true across controllers. - - - - DRAFT SUBMITTED REVIEW APPROVED EXECUTED > > > > Figure 3 -…
lessons.body:
Approval Workflows and Long-Running Processes
Enterprise systems contain processes that live longer than one HTTP request. Model the workflow explicitly instead of
scattering booleans such as approved=true across controllers.

-                            -                          -                             -
DRAFT                    SUBMITTED                    REVIEW                    APPROVED                  EXECUTED
>                            >                          >                             >
Figure 3 - A workflow is a state machine with actors, transitions, and evidence

Workflow design checklist
• Define states, allowed transitions, actor/permission requirements, transition preconditions, timestamps, reason/comments, and
terminal states.

• Put transition rules in one authoritative backend policy/service; the UI only presents actions that may be available.

• Use explicit actions such as submit(), approve(), reject(), cancel(), finalize() instead of generic update({status}).

Long-running workflow
• An approval may wait hours or days. Persist workflow state; do not keep it in memory or an HTTP connection.

• For multi-step asynchronous work, store progress and make each step restartable. Background workers can continue after process
restarts.
approvePurchaseOrder(poId, actor) {
assertPermission(actor, "po.approve")
assertState(po, "SUBMITTED")
assertApprovalThreshold(actor, po.total)
return transition(po, "APPROVED")
}

An approval is a business transition, not merely a status field edit.
Source basis: application state-machine/workflow design; persisted state is required for long-running business processes.

lessons.title: Audit Trails History and Effective Dates
lessons.summary: Audit Trails, History, and Effective Dates Enterprise data often needs an answer to “who changed what, when, why, and from which business state?” That is different from ordinary application logging. Business - - - - Investigation / Transaction Domain row Audit record command > >…
lessons.body:
Audit Trails, History, and Effective Dates
Enterprise data often needs an answer to “who changed what, when, why, and from which business state?” That is
different from ordinary application logging.

Business         -                          -                         -                         -      Investigation /
Transaction               Domain row                Audit record
command          >                          >                         >                         >          report

Figure 4 - Audit evidence is durable business data

Audit record
• Capture actor identity, action, entity type/id, timestamp, relevant before/after or structured change data, reason, requestId/correlation,
and business context.

• Write critical audit evidence in the same transaction as the business change when atomicity is required.

• Do not treat console/Sentry logs as the authoritative business audit ledger; operational telemetry can expire or be sampled.

Effective-dated data
• HR salary, employment status, tax settings, and organization assignments often change "effective from" a date rather than by
overwriting history.

• Prefer explicit effectiveFrom/effectiveTo or versioned records when historical reconstruction is a business requirement.
Logs explain system behavior; audit records explain business accountability. They overlap, but they are not interchangeable.
Source basis: enterprise audit/accountability architecture; distinguish durable audit records from sampled operational telemetry.

lessons.summary: Background Jobs, Idempotency, and Retries Payroll calculation, report generation, imports, email batches, document generation, and integrations should not turn user-facing HTTP requests into long-running processes. - - - - - Notify / query HTTP command Persist intent Enqueue job Worker Persist result > > >…
lessons.body:
Background Jobs, Idempotency, and Retries
Payroll calculation, report generation, imports, email batches, document generation, and integrations should not turn
user-facing HTTP requests into long-running processes.

-                         -                         -                         -                          -     Notify / query
HTTP command                Persist intent            Enqueue job                  Worker                 Persist result
>                         >                         >                         >                          >        status

Figure 5 - Long work moves to durable workers while the API remains responsive

2026 course line
• @nestjs/bullmq 12.0.0 integrates BullMQ with NestJS 12; BullMQ 6.x is the current major queue line.

• Jobs must be designed for retries. BullMQ explicitly recommends idempotent jobs so retrying a failed job leads to the same final state
as a successful first attempt.

• Use stable business idempotency keys/job IDs where duplicate execution would be harmful, but remember queue de-duplication alone
is not a complete business idempotency strategy.

Examples
• Generate payroll PDF, import attendance CSV, synchronize government contribution tables, send approved PO to supplier integration,
rebuild reporting projection.

• Recurring work should use the current BullMQ Job Scheduler API rather than removed legacy repeatable-job APIs in BullMQ 6.
job key: payroll-run:<runId>:calculate

Worker checks database:
- already COMPLETED? return existing result
- PROCESSING stale? recover according to policy
- otherwise claim work and continue

Retry is safe only when the operation is designed to survive duplicate delivery and partial failure.
Official references: BullMQ idempotent jobs https://docs.bullmq.io/patterns/idempotent-jobs ; Job Schedulers https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/job-schedulers/
; npm @nestjs/bullmq 12.0.0.

lessons.summary: Financial Correctness: Payroll and Accounting Financial systems need stronger invariants than ordinary CRUD. Monetary arithmetic, finalization, periods, rounding, and reproducibility must be explicit business rules. Money rules • Never use binary floating-point for authoritative monetary amounts. PostgreSQL numeric/decimal is exact and selectable in precision; PostgreSQL…
lessons.body:
Financial Correctness: Payroll and Accounting
Financial systems need stronger invariants than ordinary CRUD. Monetary arithmetic, finalization, periods, rounding,
and reproducibility must be explicit business rules.

Money rules
• Never use binary floating-point for authoritative monetary amounts. PostgreSQL numeric/decimal is exact and selectable in precision;
PostgreSQL also warns against floating point for money because of rounding risk.

• Define currency, scale, rounding mode, and when rounding occurs. Do not let UI formatting decide accounting behavior.

• Persist calculation inputs/version references needed to reproduce a finalized payroll or journal result.

Finalize means something
• DRAFT calculations may be recomputed. FINALIZED payroll/journal results should normally be immutable; corrections are new
adjustment/reversal records, not silent edits.

• Accounting journal entries require balanced debits and credits before posting; closed periods reject ordinary postings.

• PayrollRun should have a deterministic lifecycle: DRAFT -> CALCULATING -> REVIEW -> FINALIZED -> PAID/ARCHIVED as
appropriate.
model MoneyExample {
amount Decimal @db.Decimal(18, 2)
currency String @db.VarChar(3)
}

# Never store authoritative payroll money in float/double.

Financial correctness is a domain invariant, not a formatting concern.
Official reference: PostgreSQL 18 numeric is exact; floating point should not be used for money due to rounding risk -
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype-money.html

lessons.summary: Procurement, Inventory, and Stock Consistency Procurement and inventory illustrate why enterprise systems need ledgers, reservations, and transaction boundaries rather than one mutable “quantity” field. - - - - - Accounting Requisition PO Receive Stock movement Available stock > > > > > impact Figure 6…
lessons.body:
Procurement, Inventory, and Stock Consistency
Procurement and inventory illustrate why enterprise systems need ledgers, reservations, and transaction boundaries
rather than one mutable “quantity” field.

-                         -                         -                         -                       -   Accounting
Requisition                   PO                      Receive              Stock movement             Available stock
>                         >                         >                         >                       >     impact

Figure 6 - Physical and financial consequences cross module boundaries

Stock model
• Use StockMovement as durable evidence: RECEIPT, ISSUE, TRANSFER, ADJUSTMENT, RETURN. Current balance can be
derived/materialized from movement history.

• If reservations exist, distinguish onHand, reserved, and available rather than subtracting arbitrary UI values.

• Validate source/destination, item status, quantity sign, authorization, and sufficient stock under a transaction/concurrency strategy.

Procurement consistency
• Received quantity cannot exceed the allowed ordered quantity without an explicit variance policy.

• PO approval authority may depend on amount, department, budget, category, and segregation-of-duties rules.

• Goods receipt should be linked to its PO lines and later accounting/payables process, not represented as an unrelated stock edit.
A stock balance is the result of controlled movements; the movement ledger is the evidence.
Source basis: transactional inventory/procurement modeling principles; exact policies vary by organization and regulation.

lessons.title: Integration Boundaries Events and Outbox
lessons.summary: Integration Boundaries, Events, and the Outbox Pattern Enterprise systems integrate with banks, biometrics, email/SMS, government services, accounting systems, suppliers, and identity providers. External side effects cannot participate in the same database transaction. Business - - - - Inbox/idempoten Outbox row Publisher/worker External system transaction >…
lessons.body:
Integration Boundaries, Events, and the Outbox
Pattern
Enterprise systems integrate with banks, biometrics, email/SMS, government services, accounting systems, suppliers,
and identity providers. External side effects cannot participate in the same database transaction.

Business          -                          -                           -                           -   Inbox/idempoten
Outbox row               Publisher/worker            External system
transaction        >                          >                           >                           >          cy

Figure 7 - Persist intent before performing unreliable external side effects

Boundary rule
• Do not call an external provider halfway through a database transaction and assume both systems commit atomically.

• Persist the business change and an outbox/integration intent atomically; a worker publishes/sends after commit and records delivery
state.

• Inbound webhooks should verify authenticity, store a stable provider/event ID, and process idempotently so duplicate delivery cannot
duplicate business effects.

Event design
• Use business events such as PurchaseOrderApproved or PayrollRunFinalized, not low-level "row updated" messages as the default
integration contract.

• Keep event payloads versionable and avoid leaking internal ORM row shapes to external consumers.
BEGIN TRANSACTION
update purchase_order set status = 'APPROVED'
insert audit_event (...)
insert integration_outbox (event_type, aggregate_id, payload)
COMMIT

worker -> supplier/accounting integration

The outbox solves "database committed but message was never sent" by making publish intent durable.
Source basis: transactional outbox/inbox architectural pattern; external systems cannot share a local PostgreSQL atomic transaction.

Reporting, Read Models, and Exports
Operational screens and enterprise reports have different query needs. Do not distort transactional models only to make
one heavy report convenient.

Transactional      -                         -                         -                         -       Storage /
Projection / query           Report job                  Artifact
tables          >                         >                         >                         >       download

Figure 8 - Heavy reporting can use purpose-built reads and background execution

Reporting strategy
• Start with indexed SQL queries and purpose-built repository projections. Use views/materialized projections/read models when
repeated reporting pressure justifies them.

• Large PDF/Excel exports belong in background jobs; persist report status and generated artifact metadata instead of holding an HTTP
request open.

• Reports must apply the same tenant/department/security scope as interactive APIs.

Enterprise considerations
• Financial and payroll reports often need "as-of" historical data, not whatever the current mutable row contains.

• For management analytics, separate operational correctness from analytics latency. A slightly delayed read model may be acceptable
if clearly documented.
A report is another product surface with security, correctness, performance, and reproducibility requirements.
Source basis: CQRS/read-model concepts applied pragmatically; use only when operational queries/reporting pressure justifies it.

lessons.body:
Enterprise Permissions and Segregation of Duties
OWNER/ADMIN/MEMBER is sufficient for TaskFlow, but enterprise systems often need permission scopes,
organizational context, approval limits, and segregation of duties.

Concern                          Example                                             Policy owner

Role                             Payroll Officer                                     Authorization policy

Scope                            Company / branch / department                       Membership / org assignment

Permission                       payroll.finalize                                    Permission matrix

Limit                            approve PO <= 100,000                               Business authorization rule

Relationship                     Supervisor of employee                              Resource/context policy

SoD                              Creator cannot final-approve own PO                 Business security rule

Decision model
• Authenticate identity first, resolve enterprise user and organizational scope, then evaluate permission plus resource/business context.

• Keep high-risk operations default-deny. UI visibility is convenience; backend policy is enforcement.

• Log/audit sensitive authorization outcomes such as payroll finalization, role changes, approval overrides, and period reopening.
Enterprise authorization is often RBAC + scope + relationship + business rule, not RBAC alone.
Source basis: Phase 19 authorization model extended with organization scope, approval limits, and segregation-of-duties business rules.

lessons.body:
Scaling and Migration Without a Rewrite
The TaskFlow architecture is intentionally replaceable. Scale the constrained boundary first, then extract only where
independent operation creates more value than distributed-system cost.

-                         -                          -        Selective      -     Cloud/on-prem
Modular monolith              Workers                 Read models
>                         >                          >        services       >        options

Figure 9 - Evolution is incremental and evidence-driven

Typical evolution
• Vercel web can remain independent while NestJS API/workers scale separately.

• Move long work to BullMQ workers before splitting business modules into network services.

• Supabase PostgreSQL can migrate to self-hosted/AWS PostgreSQL because Prisma/application services do not depend on
dashboard-only business logic.

• Supabase Storage can migrate behind an application-owned storage adapter to S3-compatible storage; Redis/Upstash can move to
self-hosted/managed Redis.

Service extraction trigger
• Extract when a module needs independent scaling, release, resilience, compliance, or team ownership and has a stable contract/data
boundary.

• After extraction, accept new costs: network failure, distributed tracing, eventual consistency, deployment coordination, contract
versioning, and data ownership.
Microservices are a trade, not an upgrade. A well-modularized monolith can support very serious systems.
Source basis: Phase 35 dependency boundaries plus replaceable infrastructure strategy. Service extraction requires operational evidence.

The final exercise is to convert one enterprise domain into an implementable architecture using the same reasoning
applied throughout TaskFlow.

Choose domain            Model invariants           Design modules             Define workflows                                 Test/operate
>                        >                            >                        >   jobs/integrations   >
Figure 10 - Final capstone: architecture from business rules outward

Capstone options
• Government/private HRIS with timekeeping, leave, payroll, deductions, recruitment, audit logs, and reports.

• Procurement + inventory with requisitions, approvals, suppliers, POs, receiving, stock movements, reservations, and accounting
handoff.

• Accounting/financial management with chart of accounts, journals, periods, approvals, reconciliation, reporting, and audit evidence.

Required deliverables
• Module map and dependency rules; key entities and invariants; approval/state machines; permission matrix; transaction boundaries;
job/idempotency plan; integration contracts; audit strategy; reporting path; failure/recovery model; deployment/observability plan.

• Identify what remains synchronous, what becomes a worker, and what evidence would justify service extraction later.

• Write ADRs for the three highest-impact decisions and a migration plan from the current TaskFlow-shaped platform.

Course exit standard
• You should now be able to explain why each layer exists, where a rule belongs, how to verify it, and how to evolve it without blindly
copying a framework architecture diagram.
The course is complete when you can design the next system from first principles, not when you can reproduce TaskFlow
from memory.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 36: TaskFlow -> Enterprise Systems

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
business capabilities -> modular monolith -> workflow/state machines -> transactional boundaries -> outbox/events -> background workers -> reporting/integrations -> scale-out only when earned

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Microservices before module boundaries are understood
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Boolean fields replacing explicit workflow states
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — TaskFlow -> Enterprise Systems

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 36 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Generalize TaskFlow patterns into larger enterprise systems while preserving modular boundaries, workflows, auditability, integration reliability, and migration paths.

Required artifact
Enterprise expansion blueprint for an HRIS/procurement/inventory/payroll-style system with modules, workflows, events, audit, and scaling triggers.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can decompose by business capability.
• Can model long-running workflows.
• Can explain outbox/event reliability.
• Can justify when distribution is and is not earned.

Independent build sequence
1. Choose one enterprise domain and identify business capabilities before choosing services/databases.
2. Design modules with explicit ownership and public interfaces inside a modular monolith.
3. Model one long-running approval as a state machine with actors, transitions, evidence, and audit records.
4. Identify a transaction that crosses an integration boundary and design an outbox/event handoff.
5. Separate synchronous user requests from background work such as reports, imports, notifications, or payroll runs.
6. Write concrete scaling triggers that would justify extracting a service, queue, cache, or separate database later.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

# Approval Workflow Template

## States
DRAFT -> SUBMITTED -> REVIEW -> APPROVED -> EXECUTED

## For each transition define
- command name
- allowed source state
- target state
- actor permission
- organizational scope
- monetary/other approval limits
- preconditions
- required reason/comment
- audit event
- side effects / queued work

Never expose a generic API that lets a client assign any workflow state directly.

# Audit Event Schema

Suggested fields:

- id
- occurredAt
- actorUserId / auth subject
- workspace/company/department context
- action
- entityType
- entityId
- reason
- beforeJson (only appropriate fields)
- afterJson (only appropriate fields)
- requestId / correlationId
- source (WEB/API/JOB/INTEGRATION)

For critical changes, write the audit event in the same database transaction as the business change. Do not put credentials or unnecessary sensitive data into audit payloads.

# Final Enterprise Capstone Blueprint

Choose HRIS, Procurement+Inventory, or Accounting. Produce:

1. Module/bounded-context map.
2. Key entities and invariants.
3. State/approval workflows.
4. Permission + scope + segregation-of-duties matrix.
5. Transaction boundaries.
6. Audit-event model.
7. Background-job and idempotency plan.
8. Integration contracts and outbox/inbox strategy.
9. Reporting/read-model strategy.
10. Test matrix and failure-recovery cases.
11. Deployment/observability plan.
12. ADRs for the three highest-impact architecture decisions.
13. Evidence/triggers that would justify future service extraction.

# Domain Module Catalog

| Module | Owns | Example commands |
|---|---|---|
| People | Employee/employment/org assignments | hireEmployee, transferEmployee, terminateEmployment |
| Leave | Leave balances and requests | submitLeave, approveLeave, cancelLeave |
| Payroll | Payroll runs/pay items/deductions | calculatePayroll, finalizePayroll, markPaid |
| Procurement | Requisitions/POs/suppliers | submitRequisition, approvePO, cancelPO |
| Inventory | Items/warehouses/movements | receiveStock, issueStock, transferStock |
| Accounting | Accounts/journals/periods | postJournal, closePeriod, reverseJournal |
| Recruitment | Openings/applicants/offers | advanceApplicant, approveOffer, hireApplicant |

Each module exports a small public service/event contract. Do not expose repositories or Prisma models as the default cross-module API.

# Enterprise Architecture Map

```text
Next.js
  -> NestJS/Fastify modular application
      -> People / Payroll / Leave / Procurement / Inventory / Accounting / Recruitment
      -> Repository interfaces / Prisma implementations
      -> PostgreSQL
      -> BullMQ workers for long-running work
      -> Supabase Auth / Storage / Realtime where applicable
```

Start as a modular monolith. Extract workers or services only when scaling, reliability, compliance, release cadence, or team ownership creates real pressure.

# Enterprise Permission Matrix - Example

| Role | Scope | Example permissions | Extra constraints |
|---|---|---|---|
| HR Officer | company/department | employee.read, leave.review | cannot edit payroll result |
| Payroll Officer | company | payroll.calculate, payslip.generate | finalization may require second approver |
| Supervisor | team | leave.approve, employee.read.team | relationship-scoped |
| Procurement Officer | business unit | requisition.manage, po.create | cannot final approve own PO |
| Department Head | department | po.approve | approval amount threshold |
| Accounting | company | journal.post, period.read | closed-period rule |

Authorization decision = identity + scope + permission + relationship + business rule.

# Financial Correctness Checklist

- Use exact decimal/numeric amounts, never binary float for authoritative money.
- Store currency explicitly.
- Define rounding mode and rounding stage.
- Version tables/formulas/rates used for payroll calculations.
- Finalized payroll/journals should be immutable; corrections use adjustments/reversals.
- Journal entries must balance before posting.
- Closed accounting periods reject normal postings.
- Recalculation must be reproducible from durable inputs/version references.

# Idempotency and Background Jobs

Course line:
- @nestjs/bullmq 12.0.0
- BullMQ 6.x

## Example job key
`payroll-run:<runId>:calculate`

## Worker rule
1. Load durable operation state.
2. If already completed, return the durable result.
3. Claim/process according to concurrency policy.
4. Persist progress/results.
5. Make external side effects independently idempotent.

BullMQ recommends idempotent jobs so retries converge to the same final state. BullMQ 6 uses Job Schedulers for recurring work.

# Integration Boundaries

## Outbound
Business transaction -> outbox row -> worker -> external provider -> delivery state.

## Inbound webhook
Verify authenticity -> persist provider event ID -> deduplicate -> process business command -> persist result.

## Contract rule
Use business events such as `PurchaseOrderApproved` and version their payloads. Avoid publishing raw Prisma rows as long-lived external contracts.

# Migration Roadmap

## Stage 1 - Modular monolith
Single API, explicit Nest feature modules, one PostgreSQL cluster.

## Stage 2 - Worker separation
BullMQ workers for payroll calculation, imports, exports, notification batches, integrations.

## Stage 3 - Read scaling
Indexes, read models, replicas/analytics pipeline where evidence requires.

## Stage 4 - Selective service extraction
Only modules with independent scale/reliability/team/compliance pressure.

## Infrastructure replacement path
- Supabase PostgreSQL -> self-hosted/AWS PostgreSQL
- Supabase Storage -> S3-compatible storage adapter
- Upstash/managed Redis -> alternate Redis
- Railway/Render -> AWS containers/Kubernetes when operations justify it

# TaskFlow Enterprise Systems Blueprint

This is the final course reference snapshot. It does not turn TaskFlow into one giant ERP implementation. Instead it provides reusable architecture templates for evolving the same principles into HRIS, payroll, procurement, inventory, accounting, recruitment, and other enterprise modules.

The default evolution strategy is:
1. modular monolith,
2. durable background workers,
3. purpose-built read models,
4. selective service extraction only when evidence justifies it.

# Reporting Architecture

Start simple:
1. Indexed PostgreSQL query.
2. Purpose-built projection/select.
3. View/materialized read model if repeated pressure justifies it.
4. Background job for large Excel/PDF exports.
5. Store generated artifact metadata; Storage holds bytes.

Always apply tenant/department authorization to reports and exports. Historical reports must use effective-dated/versioned business data where required.

# Phase 36 Sources

Official references consulted:

- NestJS Modules: https://docs.nestjs.com/modules
- BullMQ Idempotent Jobs: https://docs.bullmq.io/patterns/idempotent-jobs
- BullMQ Job IDs/Deduplication: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/job-ids
- BullMQ Job Schedulers: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/job-schedulers/
- BullMQ Flows: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/flows/
- @nestjs/bullmq npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@nestjs/bullmq
- BullMQ npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/bullmq
- PostgreSQL 18 Monetary Types: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype-money.html
- PostgreSQL 18 Data Types (`numeric` / `decimal` exact numeric): https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype.html

Architecture patterns such as modular monoliths, transactional outbox/inbox, effective-dated history, segregation of duties, and read models are presented as engineering patterns; their exact implementation must follow the target organization's regulatory and business requirements.

# Phase 36 Version Notes

Existing course locks remain:
- Next.js 16.x
- NestJS 12.x
- Fastify 5.x
- Prisma 7.9.1 (hard course lock)
- PostgreSQL 18 line
- Zod 4.x
- TanStack Query 5.x

New enterprise-worker line verified for this phase:
- @nestjs/bullmq 12.0.0
- BullMQ 6.x (current npm line observed: 6.3.x)

Do not auto-upgrade these inside an existing course checkpoint. Verify release notes and tests first.

# Enterprise Test Matrix

| Risk | Minimum verification |
|---|---|
| Unauthorized payroll finalization | HTTP E2E + permission policy test |
| Duplicate payroll job delivery | idempotency integration test |
| PO creator self-approves despite SoD | authorization/business policy test |
| Stock transfer partially commits | PostgreSQL transaction/failure integration test |
| Accounting journal unbalanced | pure policy + service test |
| Closed-period posting | service + HTTP E2E |
| Webhook delivered twice | inbox/idempotency integration test |
| Outbox publish fails after DB commit | worker recovery test |
| Report leaks another department | real PostgreSQL scoped query + E2E |
| Audit record missing on critical command | transaction integration test |
| Finalized payroll mutated | repository/service invariant test |
| Worker retry exposes duplicate external side effect | integration contract/idempotency test |
